title: Which Jobs Can Be Replaced Today:  Fryderyk Wiatrowski and Peter Albert
talk_summary: Two founders of an agent startup argue that reactive, rule-based jobs (customer support, meeting scheduling) will be replaced first by agents triggered from a pool of events (email, Slack, Linear) rather than by prompting, and that browser agents are the generic action layer. The second half is a practical prompting/optimization ladder: prompt hygiene, task decomposition with explicit state, then fine-tuning and RL only when needed.

takeaways.technique: Rewrite prompts with an LLM and use XML delimiters
takeaways.what_they_do: They have a language model rewrite their own prompts to remove human ambiguity and low-complexity phrasing, and use XML tags to separate instructions from content.
takeaways.evidence_quote: usually it's a good idea to kind of rewrite your prompts with language models itself

takeaways.technique: Treat all prompt content as noise; minimize and structure it
takeaways.what_they_do: They assume everything in the prompt is noise plus a little signal, so they strip context to only what's relevant and keep few-shot examples short (only the important parts of long examples).
takeaways.evidence_quote: everything that you put in prompt is basically noise and and some valuable cont in there

takeaways.technique: Explicit state tracking and scratchpad for long tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: For long multi-step tasks they add explicit state tracking, planning/replanning, verification steps, and a scratchpad for intermediate work to raise context quality.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you add explicit State tracking of like if you have a longer task you basically keep track of the state

takeaways.technique: Key-value / full-rewrite tool interfaces instead of diffs
takeaways.what_they_do: They design tool calls as key-value updates (mimicking Python dict updates) or full rewrites rather than small diffs, because models are weak at generating small diffs and this splits the reasoning into two simpler steps.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you should try to avoid any recursive n structures if you can

takeaways.what_they_do: As soon as they start prompting they set up 10-20 examples that every prompt change is run against, plus end-to-end evals.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to already set up some maybe like 10 20 examples to kind of always run each prom through

takeaways.what_they_do: They propose aggregating all triggers (email, Slack, Linear issues, market events) into one pool that agents poll and act on by rules, with human approval before action, rather than humans prompting agents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the first step to implementing the reactive um drop replacement by agents is to create a pool of triggers
